content: Molecular evidence indicates that visceral leishmaniasis is expanding into non-program districts of Nepal, as reported in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2019. Alvar et al. (2012) provided global estimates of leishmaniasis incidence in PLOS ONE, highlighting its widespread impact. The World Health Organization (WHO) has convened multiple meetings and developed strategic frameworks to address neglected tropical diseases, including kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), with a focus on elimination and eradication efforts in South-East Asia and globally. The WHO's regional strategies for kala-azar elimination, spanning 2005–2015 and 2011–2015, emphasized cross-border collaboration and surveillance. Updated frameworks for 2022–2026 aim to accelerate and sustain elimination efforts. Hirve et al. (2017) discussed translating research into public health practices for visceral leishmaniasis in the Indian subcontinent in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The WHO's 2022 guidelines address treatment for visceral leishmaniasis in HIV co-infected patients in East Africa and South-East Asia. Studies have validated diagnostic algorithms for visceral leishmaniasis in elimination settings, such as Cloots et al. (2022) in Diagnostics (Basel). Research by Cloots et al. (2021) in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology identified HIV co-infection as a predictor of increased leishmania transmission in Bihar, India. Dixit et al. (2020) and Ghosh et al. (2018) advanced molecular diagnostic methods for post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), with real-time PCR evaluations in endemic areas like Bangladesh. Goyal et al. (2020) examined long-term relapse rates and PKDL incidence following different treatment regimens for visceral leishmaniasis in Bihar, India, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. Burza et al. (2014) identified risk factors for relapse in immunocompetent patients treated with liposomal amphotericin B in Bihar. Singh et al. (2021) conducted a transmission dynamics study using xenodiagnosis to evaluate human infectiousness to sandflies in visceral leishmaniasis-endemic areas, published in The Lancet Microbe. The WHO has emphasized sustainable surveillance for neglected tropical diseases in the post-elimination era, as discussed by Hatherell et al. (2021) in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The organization has also developed a roadmap for neglected tropical diseases (2021–2030) and a strategic framework for integrated control of skin-related neglected tropical diseases (2022). Efforts to improve kala-azar case management include sentinel site surveillance systems in Bihar, as reported by Das et al. (2021) in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. Dubey et al. (2021) evaluated active case detection methods to support elimination in India, published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Priest et al. (2016) integrated multiplex bead assays for parasitic diseases into national serosurveys in Cambodia, as reported in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The WHO has conducted independent assessments of kala-azar elimination programs in India and issued position statements on integrated vector management. Cross-border collaboration for kala-azar and malaria elimination along the borders of India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Nepal was reviewed in a 2021 virtual meeting. Participants agreed on priorities such as signing cross-border collaboration agreements, establishing communication channels, and ensuring universal access to quality diagnosis, treatment, and prevention services. Recommended treatment regimens for kala-azar include liposomal amphotericin B, combination therapies (e.g., liposomal amphotericin B with miltefosine or paromomycin), and pentavalent antimonials in areas where they remain effective. Rescue treatments involve higher doses of liposomal amphotericin B or conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate. For PKDL, treatment options include amphotericin B deoxycholate or miltefosine. These recommendations are based on WHO guidelines and expert committee reports.
